notes: PART 1 of 2 — merged by tools/generate_pack.py being run on both parts (same pack name; codes continue by track prefix). The state's own OS edition: Louisiana's river, coast, energy, ports and agriculture taught as curriculum, joined by part 2's culture tracks. Facts are public-record Louisiana; transfer checks are phrased against the learner's own parish so they stay true everywhere in the state. 10 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 500 blocks total across both parts.

tracks.name: The river: the Mississippi and its machinery

themes.theme: A continent's drain runs past your door
themes.description: The Mississippi's watershed — how water from thirty-one states arrives at Louisiana, and what that makes the river carry.
themes.transfer_check: Trace, on a real map, the path rain falling in two distant states takes to pass Louisiana, and name what it picks up on the way.

themes.description: The mainline levees from the river's own banks — what they protect, what they stopped, and what confining a river costs downstream.
themes.transfer_check: Visit or study the levee section nearest your parish and report who maintains it, its height history, and what sits behind it.

themes.theme: The structures that hold the river in place
themes.description: Old River Control and the spillways — the machinery that keeps the Mississippi in its channel and away from the Atchafalaya's shorter path.
themes.transfer_check: Explain, with a drawing, what Old River Control does and what would change downstream if it failed, verified against an authoritative source.

themes.description: Bonnet Carré and Morganza — when a spillway opens, who decides, and what the fresh water does to the basins it enters.
themes.transfer_check: From records of one real spillway opening, chart the trigger, the decision-maker, and two documented downstream effects.

themes.description: River stages, flood stage and the forecast — reading the river's actual numbers the way river communities do.
themes.transfer_check: Read the current stage at the gauge nearest your parish, compare it to flood stage and the record, and state what today's number means.

themes.theme: The sediment the coast is starving for
themes.description: Mud as treasure — how the leveed river sends land-building sediment off the shelf, and the diversions meant to reclaim it.
themes.transfer_check: Explain the sediment argument for and against one real diversion project, citing each side's own documents.

themes.theme: The river as a working road
themes.description: Tows, barges and pilots — what actually moves on the river, and why one barge tow replaces dozens of trucks.
themes.transfer_check: Observe or study one real stretch of river traffic and report what was moving, in what, and roughly what it would take by road.

themes.description: The intakes, treatment and saltwater wedge — the communities that drink the Mississippi and what threatens the tap.
themes.transfer_check: Determine whether your own parish drinks river water, and for one that does, trace the intake-to-tap path and its named risks.

themes.description: America's largest river swamp — the basin, its floodway job, and the crawfish economy inside it.
themes.transfer_check: Map the Atchafalaya Basin's floodway role and profile one real livelihood that depends on the basin staying wet.

themes.theme: Living in the shadow of the river
themes.description: The capstone: river decisions as parish decisions — levees, diversions, traffic and water, argued with real neighbours.
themes.transfer_check: Run or present a structured deliberation on one real river decision affecting your region, and deliver the recommendation you would defend.

tracks.name: The working coast: wetlands and restoration

themes.description: Marsh, swamp, ridge and bayou — reading the coastal landscape's parts and what each does for the state behind it.
themes.transfer_check: Identify marsh, swamp and ridge on real imagery of the Louisiana coast and state one protective job each performs.

themes.description: Coastal land loss — the causes stacked together (subsidence, channels, levees, storms, sea rise) and the honest arithmetic of what is going.
themes.transfer_check: Compare historical and current imagery of one real coastal spot and quantify what has gone, attributing causes from published analysis.

themes.description: Surge protection, nurseries and livelihoods — what a mile of marsh is worth to a town it fronts.
themes.transfer_check: For one real coastal community, explain what the fronting wetlands do for it in a storm, citing the protection estimates.

themes.description: The state's fifty-year plan — how projects are chosen, funded and ranked, and how to read it as a citizen.
themes.transfer_check: From the current Master Plan's own documents, summarise the project nearest your parish — type, cost, purpose, status.

themes.description: Dredge, diversion and terrace — the restoration toolbox, what each technique builds, and what each costs.
themes.transfer_check: Match three real restoration projects to their techniques and report what each has measurably built so far.

themes.description: Shrimp, oyster, crab and finfish — the working coast's harvest, and how restoration and salinity decisions land on the deck.
themes.transfer_check: Profile one real Louisiana fishery — season, method, landing figures — and one live decision currently affecting it, from both sides.

themes.theme: The oyster and the salinity line
themes.description: The oyster as an animal with an address — why fresh and salt must balance, and what moves the line.
themes.transfer_check: Explain what a named freshwater event did to a real oyster area, using landings or lease records as evidence.

themes.theme: Communities deciding to stay or go
themes.description: The hardest coastal question — elevation, buyouts and relocation, told through the communities already deciding.
themes.transfer_check: Study one documented Louisiana community's stay-or-move decision and present the options it faced and the choice it made, fairly.

themes.description: The restoration economy — the trades, sciences and boats the Master Plan employs, and the local routes into them.
themes.transfer_check: Map three real jobs on one restoration project — what each does, what it requires — from the project's own records or employers.

themes.description: The capstone: reading the projections honestly and arguing what your parish should ask of the plan.
themes.transfer_check: Using the Master Plan's own future maps, describe your region's projected coast and draft your parish's one-page ask of the plan.

tracks.name: The energy corridor: from well to grid

themes.description: River, feedstock and deep water — the geography that lined the Mississippi with refineries and chemical plants.
themes.transfer_check: For one real corridor facility, explain in a paragraph why it sits where it sits — river, pipeline, port — with evidence.

themes.description: Crude in, products out — distillation and units explained at working depth, without the mystery.
themes.transfer_check: Diagram a refinery's main flow from crude to three named products and explain one unit's job to somebody else.

themes.description: Liquefaction, the terminals and the cryogenic chain — why Louisiana became an export coast and what a loading arm does.
themes.transfer_check: Explain the LNG chain from pipeline gas to loaded ship, and locate the terminals on a real map with their parishes named.

themes.description: The buried network — how pipelines are marked, mapped and struck, and the call made before any digging.
themes.transfer_check: Use the official locator process for a real or staged dig on a real parcel, and read the pipeline markers nearest your parish.

themes.description: The maintenance surges that employ thousands — what a turnaround is, the crafts it calls, and how workers plug in.
themes.transfer_check: Profile one real turnaround's scale and crafts from public sources, and map how a qualified local worker actually gets hired onto one.

themes.description: Living next to industry — monitoring, alerts, shelter-in-place, and the community's lawful levers on permits.
themes.transfer_check: For one real fence-line community, find its monitoring data and alert system, and demonstrate the shelter-in-place response.

themes.theme: The safety culture that keeps hands
themes.description: Process safety, permits-to-work and the refusal that is a duty — the corridor's safety systems as working practice.
themes.transfer_check: Walk a staged permit-to-work for a simple task — hazards named, isolations listed, sign-offs in order — and name the stop-work right.

themes.theme: The grid the plants and parishes share
themes.description: Generation, the big substations and hurricane hardening — Louisiana's electricity from plant to parish line.
themes.transfer_check: Trace your parish's power from its likely generation source through one named substation, and report the utility's storm-hardening work there.

themes.description: Hydrogen, carbon capture and offshore wind — the projects actually proposed here, read without slogans.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real announced transition project in Louisiana and examine its claims, funding and status from primary documents.

themes.description: The capstone: process tech, crafts and the two-year path — mapping a real corridor career from a parish high school.
themes.transfer_check: Map one complete real route from your parish's high school to a named corridor job — program, cost, credential, starting pay — from the providers' own information.

themes.theme: The port complex nobody sees whole
themes.description: From Baton Rouge to the Gulf — the string of ports that together move more tonnage than almost anywhere, and what each handles.
themes.transfer_check: Name the major Louisiana ports on a real map with each one's main cargo, citing the ports' own figures.

themes.description: The elevators — how the Midwest's grain arrives by barge and leaves by ship, and why this stretch of river feeds the world.
themes.transfer_check: Explain the barge-to-elevator-to-ship chain for grain with real tonnage figures from one named elevator or port.

themes.theme: The container and the box economy
themes.description: What a container changes, how a terminal works, and where Louisiana's boxes come from and go.
themes.transfer_check: Follow one real imported product from ship to shelf through a Louisiana gateway, naming each handling step.

themes.description: Bar pilots and river pilots — why deep-draft ships change hands at the mouth, and what the pilot actually does on the bridge.
themes.transfer_check: Describe the pilotage handoffs a ship makes from the Gulf to Baton Rouge and what each pilot group's charge covers.

themes.description: Draft, shoaling and the dredges that keep the river open — depth as a thing that must be bought continuously.
themes.transfer_check: Report the current controlling depth of the river channel and what one real dredging campaign cost and achieved.

themes.theme: Port jobs and the union hall
themes.description: Longshore work, warehousing, trucking and the halls and schools that fill them — the waterfront as employer.
themes.transfer_check: Map three real port-adjacent jobs — entry route, credential, starting pay — from the actual employers, halls or programs.

themes.description: Barge to rail to truck — where cargo changes modes, and why the yard is where logistics is won or lost.
themes.transfer_check: For one real Louisiana intermodal facility, diagram a load's path across modes and identify the step most likely to delay it.

themes.description: Closing the river — hurricane port condition stages, the fleet's refuge, and restarting commerce after landfall.
themes.transfer_check: From records of one real storm, chart the port's condition stages, closure and reopening timeline, and what backed up meanwhile.

themes.theme: Customs, cargo and the paper river
themes.description: Manifests, inspections and free-trade zones — the documents that move with every ton.
themes.transfer_check: Trace the paperwork one real import or export requires through a Louisiana port, naming each document and who files it.

themes.description: The capstone: port authorities as public bodies — their boards, their taxes, and the parish's seat at the table.
themes.transfer_check: Profile your nearest port authority — board, budget, current expansion — and draft the public comment your parish's interest calls for.

tracks.name: Agriculture: rice, cane and the crawfish pond

themes.description: Why rice, sugarcane, soybeans and cotton grow where they do in Louisiana — soil, water and the map they make.
themes.transfer_check: Map Louisiana's main crop belts against soil and water on real maps, and name the crops actually grown in your own parish.

themes.description: The rice year — water in, water out, harvest — and the pumps, levees and mills that make a crop of a flood.
themes.transfer_check: Chart a real rice season's calendar from planting to mill, from a grower, extension source or farm record.

themes.description: The same field twice — rice then crawfish — and the traps, boats and boils of a uniquely Louisiana aquaculture.
themes.transfer_check: Explain the rice-crawfish rotation's annual cycle and profile one real operation's season with its actual numbers.

themes.theme: Sugarcane: the year the grinding comes
themes.description: Cane's long season — planting, the autumn harvest rush, and the mills that must grind around the clock.
themes.transfer_check: Chart the cane year through grinding season for one real mill area, and explain why the harvest cannot wait.

themes.theme: The machinery of the modern farm
themes.description: Combines, laser levels, pumps and monitors — the equipment fleet, its costs, and the skills that keep it running.
themes.transfer_check: Inventory the equipment one real rice or cane operation runs, with rough costs, and demonstrate or describe one machine's field check.

themes.description: Irrigation, the aquifer and drainage districts — the water arrangements under every field.
themes.transfer_check: For one real farming area, identify where its irrigation water comes from and the body that governs the drainage, from records.

themes.description: Input costs, futures prices and the margin — why a good crop can still lose money, read from real numbers.
themes.transfer_check: Build a one-page budget for an acre of one real Louisiana crop from published costs and prices, and state its break-even.

themes.theme: Extension and the science on the tailgate
themes.description: The land-grant system — research stations, extension agents and the trial plots that change practice.
themes.transfer_check: Contact or study your parish's actual extension service and report two current recommendations it is making to local producers.

themes.theme: Weather, insurance and the year that fails
themes.description: Freeze, flood and hurricane on a farm — crop insurance, disaster programs and surviving the failed year.
themes.transfer_check: From one documented bad year, chart what a real crop lost and which programs actually paid, from the records.

themes.theme: The next generation on the land
themes.description: The capstone: getting into farming — land access, lending, young-farmer programs — mapped honestly.
themes.transfer_check: Map one realistic route for a young person in your parish into producing — land, capital, program support — from real sources, with its hardest obstacle named.
